evidence.label: Nonhomeomorphic closed aspherical four-manifolds with the same homotopy type

headline: A paper claims two closed aspherical 4-manifolds with the same homotopy type but no homeomorphism, against Borel.
scope: Closed connected aspherical topological four-manifolds with one word-hyperbolic fundamental group; dimension four only.
plain: An aspherical manifold is one whose universal cover can be shrunk to a point, so its loops decide its whole shape up to homotopy. The Borel conjecture says two such closed manifolds with the same homotopy type must be homeomorphic. The paper claims a counterexample in dimension four. It builds two such four-manifolds that are homotopy equivalent but not homeomorphic. It also claims a self-map of one of them that no homeomorphism can replace.
doesNot: This does not affect the Borel conjecture in dimensions five and up, where it is proved for large classes of groups.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Armand Borel, letter to Jean-Pierre Serre
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims a counterexample to the homeomorphism form of the Borel conjecture, in dimension four.

explanation:
Start with a cycle of 3 points, a triangle. Try to colour each point red or blue so that neighbours get different colours. Red, blue, then the third point touches both. It fails. A cycle of 2 points works at once, red then blue. Every odd cycle fails in the same way. This tiny parity fact sits at the heart of a new topology result.

First, the setting. A manifold is a space that looks like ordinary space near each point. A torus, the surface of a doughnut, is a two-dimensional example. Its universal cover is the flat plane, which can shrink to a point. A manifold with this property is called aspherical. For such a manifold, the fundamental group, its group of loops, decides its homotopy type. Homotopy type means its shape up to continuous deformation.

The Borel conjecture is usually stated as follows. Every homotopy equivalence between closed aspherical manifolds should be homotopic to a homeomorphism[1]. A homeomorphism is a perfect, reversible matching of points. A weaker form asks only that homotopy-equivalent closed aspherical manifolds be homeomorphic. The question already appears in Borel's letter to Serre of 2 May 1953[2]. It holds in dimensions one and two, and for closed orientable three-manifolds. Hsiang and Wall proved it for homotopy tori in dimensions five and up[3]. Farrell and Jones did so for closed negatively curved manifolds there[4]. Dimension four is the hard case. Bartels and Lück's four-dimensional result assumes the fundamental group is good in Freedman's sense[5]. Khan proves rigidity only up to a weaker relation called s-cobordism[6]. Separately, Davis, Hayden, Huang, Ruberman and Sunukjian found smooth examples that are homeomorphic but not diffeomorphic[7]. That is a different question.

The paper claims to disprove the weaker form in dimension four[8]. It builds two closed aspherical four-manifolds M and N. They are homotopy equivalent but not homeomorphic. Their common fundamental group is word-hyperbolic, a strong negative-curvature property of groups[9]. It also claims a homotopy equivalence of M to itself that no homeomorphism can match[10].

Here is where parity enters. The paper starts from a four-dimensional building block and looks at its cyclic covers, unwrapped copies of degree d. The boundary of the double cover can be filled by a manifold. For odd d of at least 3, it claims no filling exists[11]. A filling would give a colouring of a cycle of d points. Neighbours could never share a colour. So the colours would have to alternate around the cycle, which is impossible when the cycle is odd[12].

The obstacle is to rule out every homeomorphism, not just one homotopy class. The paper glues the blocks in two ways, giving M and N. It proves the group of outer automorphisms, the symmetries of the fundamental group, is finite[13]. Two subgroups realized on M and N then differ. They contain different numbers of elements with finite-order lifts[14]. A homeomorphism would force them to match. The proof also uses two companion constructions from other papers[15].

How sure is this? No Lean check covers this paper. No specialist review has been published. The argument depends on two companion papers, which also lack published review. Treat the counterexample as a claim.
hypeCheck: Major if correct. No Lean check and no specialist review, and the proof depends on two companion preprints that are also unreviewed.

glossary.meaning: A space that looks like ordinary flat space near every point.
A manifold whose universal cover can be shrunk continuously to a point.
The group formed by loops in a space, up to deformation.
A pair of maps between two spaces that undo each other up to continuous deformation.
A continuous matching of points between two spaces, with a continuous inverse.
A group whose geometry behaves like a negatively curved space.
The symmetries of a group, ignoring those that come from conjugating by one of its own elements.
A weaker relation than homeomorphism, in which two manifolds bound a special shared manifold one dimension higher.
